introduction-the-curse-of-dimensionality.core: Exact nearest-neighbour search compares the query against every vector, which is O(N·d) and too slow at a billion vectors. In high dimensions, space-partitioning tricks like k-d trees collapse, so we trade a little accuracy (recall) for huge speed with Approximate Nearest Neighbour (ANN) indexes.

first_principles.problem: A brute-force scan of 1B × 1,536-dim vectors takes seconds per query, but users expect under 50 ms.
truths: Distance computations scale with N and d.
In high dimensions, distances concentrate and trees stop pruning.

analogy.title: Finding the most similar book in a billion-book library
analogy.story: Reading every book is exact but takes forever. A good librarian walks you to the right shelf and is almost always right.
analogy.breaks: A librarian never says 'here's 97% of the right answer'; ANN recall is a statistical, tunable trade-off.

example.title: Brute force vs ANN

steps.label: Decision
steps.detail: Tune the index until recall meets the product's tolerance.

example.outcome: search fast enough for real-time use.

check.q: Why do k-d trees fail for embeddings?
check.a: In high dimensions distances concentrate, so the tree can't prune branches and degrades to scanning almost everything.

hnsw-hierarchical-navigable-small-world.core: HNSW builds a multi-layer proximity graph: sparse upper layers act as express highways for long jumps, and the dense bottom layer holds every vector for fine local search. A query greedily walks from the top layer down, so lookups take roughly logarithmic time.

first_principles.problem: We need sub-millisecond search with high recall, and a flat graph needs too many hops.
truths: Small-world graphs have short paths between any two nodes.
Greedy search follows the closest neighbour.
Hierarchy cuts the number of hops.
derivation: Each vector gets a **random max layer** (exponentially fewer at the top).
Connect to **M nearest neighbours** per layer.

analogy.title: Travelling by motorway, then main road, then side street
analogy.story: You take the motorway to the right region, exit to a main road, and finish on side streets.
analogy.breaks: Real roads are fixed, while HNSW graphs are memory-hungry and deletions leave holes that degrade quality.

steps.label: Pick
steps.detail: 64 meets a 0.95 recall target with low latency.

example.outcome: a recall/latency point chosen by measurement.

check.a: The size of the candidate list during search: higher means better recall but slower queries.

ivf-inverted-file-index-the-clustering-p.core: IVF clusters vectors with k-means into nlist cells. At query time it finds the nprobe closest centroids and scans only those cells, cutting work by roughly nlist/nprobe.

first_principles.problem: Scanning all 100M vectors per query is too slow, but most of them are nowhere near the query.
truths: The nearest neighbours are probably in nearby clusters.
Scanning a few clusters is cheap.
derivation: **Assign** each vector to its nearest centroid (inverted lists).
**Query**: pick the nprobe nearest centroids and scan their lists.
Raise **nprobe** to improve recall at cluster edges.

analogy.title: A filing cabinet with labelled drawers
analogy.story: You only open the drawer or two whose label best matches what you're looking for.
analogy.breaks: An item near a drawer boundary may be filed next door, which is why nprobe > 1 matters.

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: Boundary effects mean you must probe several cells.

points: Cluster, then scan a few cells.

check.a: True neighbours near cluster boundaries are assigned to adjacent cells that aren't scanned.

pq-product-quantization-the-compression-.core: Product Quantization splits each vector into m sub-vectors and replaces each with the ID of its nearest centroid from a 256-entry codebook. A 6 KB float vector becomes m bytes (e.g. 64 B), and distances are computed quickly from lookup tables.

first_principles.problem: 1B vectors × 1,536 dims × 4 bytes ≈ 6 TB, which won't fit in RAM.
truths: Memory, not compute, limits large indexes.
Approximate distances are good enough for ranking.
derivation: **Asymmetric distance**: a precomputed query-to-centroid table, summed per code.
**Re-rank** the top candidates with full vectors if needed.

analogy.title: Describing a face by picking from catalogues of eyes, noses and mouths
analogy.story: 'Eyes #41, nose #7, mouth #200' is tiny to store and close enough to recognise someone.
analogy.breaks: Compression loses detail, so recall drops; re-ranking with original vectors recovers it.

steps.label: Re-rank
steps.detail: Fetch full vectors for the top 100 to restore precision.

check.q: How many bytes does a PQ code use with m=64 and 256 centroids?
check.a: 64 bytes: one byte (256 options) per sub-vector.

the-great-trade-off-hnsw-vs-ivf-pq.core: HNSW gives the best recall and latency but needs all full vectors plus graph links in RAM. IVF-PQ is far more memory-efficient and scales to billions but has lower recall unless you re-rank. Choose by dataset size, memory budget, recall target and update pattern.

first_principles.problem: A team defaults to HNSW for 2B vectors and needs 15 TB of RAM.
truths: RAM is the dominant cost at scale.
derivation: **Hybrid**: IVF with HNSW over centroids, or HNSW+PQ.

analogy.title: A sports car versus a freight train
analogy.story: The sports car is fastest for a few passengers; the freight train moves enormous loads cheaply.
analogy.breaks: You can combine index types (e.g. HNSW over IVF centroids), which you can't do with vehicles.

example.outcome: an index that fits both budget and accuracy.
